subtype: Approach: builds the matrix in a spreadsheet and adjusts weights to see how the ranking changes [Action]
passage: Sunday night. Three offers, one spreadsheet. Columns: salary, learning, location, growth. I scored each offer 1 to 5 in every column, then set weights. First pass: salary 4, learning 3, location 2, growth 3. Offer B won, mostly on pay. Then I got curious and moved the weights around. Learning up to 5: B and C tie. Location up to 5: C wins clearly. Salary down to 1: C wins again. So C wins in almost every tilt except when salary is everything. Sent the sheet to Disha, who wrote back, 'So why did you start with pay so high?' Fair question. Tomorrow I'll ask myself whether I'm fine earning a bit less at C. — Pallavi

qa.q: Which offer won on the first pass?
qa.a: Offer B won on the first pass, mostly on pay.

qa.q: How does Pallavi feel about the result?
qa.a: Pallavi feels curious and thoughtful, and is still checking whether earning a bit less at C would be acceptable.

qa.q: What other step could Pallavi take before deciding?
qa.a: Pallavi could speak to a current employee at C about daily work, since a matrix cannot show what the days feel like.

qa.q: How might Disha have seen Pallavi's first weighting?
qa.a: Disha probably felt that pay was weighted too heavily, which is why Disha asked why Pallavi started with it so high.

grounding: Shows a student putting three job offers into a spreadsheet and changing the weights to test whether the winning offer holds up.
